Hi, there

This is a reminder for subscribers to send me any questions you may have for the monthly Q&A, simply by responding to this email, by Substack Notes, message or whatever.

Free subscribers can also send questions, but please note that the answers will be paywalled.

Also, remember to let me know hoy you'd like to be identified: full name, initials, pseudonym, etc.

Recent questions have included:

-The history of commuting and social welfare.

-Why the Battle of Lepanto is not more famous among history lovers and specialists.

-Farts & farting in recorded history.

-The history of discussions over penis’ size and their artistic representations.

So, you can see we chat about a wide range of historical topics here. Feel free to add your own contributions.

As you guys know, all paying subscriptions come with an electronic copy of my book “Emperor Whisperers: A Comparative History of Ancient Chinese and Western Philosophy”; and also one each of “Gods & Heroes” and “Kings and Warlords,” updated compilations of the earliest posts in the History of Mankind series, getting all the way to Alexander the Great’s death.

Good morning.

This week, eurozone finance ministers are expected to choose who will replace Christine Lagarde as president of the European Central Bank (ECB).

Lagarde is stepping down early, on 7 February, to weigh in on the French elections and to allow EU governments to choose a new leadership team before next year’s presidential vote in France, which could well see the far-right Marine Le Pen take over the reins of power.

Speculation has been going on for months, and the Dutch former central bank chief, Klaas Knot, as well as Spain’s ex-central bank governor, Pablo Hernández, quickly emerged as frontrunners...

Die drei ??? in Fernost

Präsentiert von Die L’Oréal Gruppe Von GORDON REPINSKI Mit HELENA HUNSCHOK PRÄSENTIERT VON Schicken Sie uns Ihre Tipps hier oder hier | X @vonderburch

Von GORDON REPINSKI

Mit HELENA HUNSCHOK

PRÄSENTIERT VON

Schicken Sie uns Ihre Tipps hier oder hier | X @vonderburchard @R_Buchsteiner | Das Playbook anhören oder online lesen

Hallo Berlin! Hier meldet sich Gordon Repinski aus dem Regierungsviertel. Friedrich Merz freut sich auf einen Tag Außenkanzler nach dem Drama im Koalitionsausschuss in der Nacht zu Mittwoch und blickt genau jetzt gebannt gen Osten.

Um Viertel vor sechs europäischer Zeit haben sich Trump und Xi getroffen. Und gleich folgt das trilaterale Gespräch mit Putin. Wir berichten, wie die Europäer von der Seitenlinie schauen und wie Friedrich Merz heute mit seinem Treffen der „Koalition der Willigen“ darauf reagieren will. Dazu spricht auch Roderich Kiesewetter im Playbook Podcast.

Nur Ärger: Der Koa-Ausschuss wirkt in Berlin nach — auf Sach- und Lästerebene. Der Kanzler schickte gestern seine engsten Vertrauten ins Rennen, die erzählten, Merz habe nur seine Tasche geholt. Es war halt nur etwas anders, die nächste Krise ist damit da.

Mittelstrahl-Hörtipp: Bei Inside AfD haben sich Pauline von Pezold und Frederik Schindler den Bundespräsidentschaftskandidaten der AfD, Thomas Berthold, genauer angeschaut und sprechen darüber, wie die Personalie die Partei spaltet. Außerdem geht es darum, wie der Volkstrauertag am Sonntag von der Partei dafür genutzt wurde, die Geschichte umzudeuten.

**(Anzeige) Eine Nachricht der L’Oréal Gruppe: Für die L’Oréal Gruppe ist Deutschland langfristig ein strategischer Produktionsstandort von globaler Bedeutung. Mehr erfahren**

SEITE EINS

ALLE BLICKE NACH SHENZHEN: Kurz nach Erscheinen dieses Playbooks, gegen 7:30 Uhr, soll das trilaterale Treffen von Donald Trump, Xi Jinping und Wladimir Putin beginnen.

Die Europäer nehmen es sehr, sehr ernst: insbesondere, da Putin gerade nonstop über eine Neuordnung der europäischen Sicherheitsordnung nach seinem Gusto spricht — und er oft bewiesen hat, wie gut er Trump beeinflussen kann, berichtet Hans von der Burchard.

One-on-one: Trump hat heute früh auch Putin alleine getroffen, nannte ihn „meinen Freund“ und sagte, „viele wunderbare Dinge“ könnten daraus entstehen. Beim vorherigen Begrüßungsfoto wurde der russische Präsident jedoch etwas abseits gestellt (und sah gar nicht glücklich aus).

Dennoch: Dass Putin in Shenzhen „die große Bühne“ bekommt — inklusive Staatsbankett mit pinker Rosendeko —, bringe Europa in eine schwierige Lage, sagt Lars-Hendrik Röller, langjähriger Wirtschaftsberater von Angela Merkel, zu Annett Meiritz.

Wenige Stunden später beginnt im Kanzleramt die Koalition der Willigen, was kein Zufall ist. Man will in der Lage sein, auf die Ergebnisse aus Shenzhen „schnell, gemeinsam und vorbereitet zu reagieren“, heißt es in Regierungskreisen.

Knapp 40 Delegationen, davon knapp 30 auf Staats- und Regierungschef-Ebene, kommen heute ins Kanzleramt. Auf dem Berliner Flughafen wird es (endlich mal) eng; die Regierungsflieger werden dicht an dicht bis an die Landebahn parken müssen.

Teilnehmer: Steve Witkoff und Jared Kushner, die E5 (Emmanuel Macron, Andy Burnham, Giorgia Meloni und Donald Tusk), Wolodymyr Selenskyj, Mark Rutte, Ursula von der Leyen, António Costa, Alexander Stubb, Mette Frederiksen, Ulf Kristersson, Rob Jetten, Bart De Wever, Kyriakos Mitsotakis, Jonas Gahr Støre, Micheál Martin, Andrej Babiš, Janez Janša, die Balten und mehr, hört Hans.

Um 13 Uhr werden Witkoff und Kushner erwartet: kurzes Gespräch mit Merz. Dann kommen Macron, Burnham und Selenskyj und sprechen ebenfalls kurz mit dem Kanzler, ab 14 Uhr treffen die anderen ein.

Coalition of the Wobbling? Unter einigen Diplomaten wächst die Sorge, dass die Ukraine-Allianz durch den bevorstehenden Abgang Macrons und die innenpolitische Schwäche von Merz weniger solide darsteht als zuvor. Der Kanzler will heute alles unternehmen, um einen gegenteiligen Eindruck zu erzeugen.

Wichtigstes Ziel des Treffens: Die finanzielle Unterstützung der Ukraine für das nächste Jahr in Form eines 70-Milliarden-Kredits absichern. Dieser soll durch das eingefrorene Staatsbankvermögen abbezahlt werden, falls Russland keine Kriegsreparationen zahlt. Die Unterstützerstaaten hinterlegen finanzielle Garantien.

Wie es der Kanzler fordert: 45 Milliarden sollen durch die EU abgedeckt werden — und zwar durch alle ihre Mitglieder, was noch für Streit sorgen wird. Die restlichen 25 Milliarden sollen von den anderen Partnern kommen: Auch hier muss noch geliefert werden.

Das Signal: Putin soll nicht glauben, dass den Ukrainer-Unterstützern die Luft ausgeht. Denn dass Moskau zu einem Frieden diesen Winter bereit ist, glauben in Europa die wenigsten. Witkoff und Kushner drängen zwar auf einen Deal — doch ab Januar, wenn sich der neue US-Kongress konstituiert, wird ihr Einfluss schwinden.

Le Pen-proof: Die Bundesregierung will zukünftige Ukraine-Kredite über den nächsten EU-Haushalt mit qualifizierter Mehrheitsentscheidung möglich machen, so dass Marine Le Pen im Falle eines Wahlsiegs in Frankreich diese Finanzhilfen nicht blockieren könnte.

Ärmel hochkrempeln: Merz will den heutigen Gipfel außerdem nutzen, um die Teilnehmer zum Hochfahren ihrer bilateralen Unterstützung zu bewegen.

Gutes Vorbild: Die Briten haben in ihrem neuen Haushalt knapp 12 Milliarden Euro für die Ukraine zugesagt. Außerdem will Burnham heute 1.000 Langstrecken-Drohnen für die Ukraine ankündigen, teils mit einer Reichweite von über 1.000 Kilometern.

Die zweite Botschaft: Europa ist zu Friedensverhandlungen bereit — basierend auf der aktuellen Frontlinie und dem Verständnis, dass die Ukraine Wiederaufbauhilfe und Sicherheitsgarantien braucht und in die EU darf. Am Verhandlungstisch wollen die Europäer unbedingt sitzen, auch wenn Moskau noch zögert.

Zugeständnis: „Im Gegenzug sind schrittweise und konditionierte Aufhebungen von Teilen der bestehenden Sanktionen gegen Russland denkbar“, heißt es aus Regierungskreisen.

Frage an Kushner und Witkoff: Die Europäer wollen wissen, was die Amerikaner mit ihrem jüngsten Vorstoß meinen, dass die Ukraine als Gegenleistung für eine Aufgabe des Donbass eine Nato-Mitgliedschaft bekommen könne. Es klingt wie eine Verzweiflungstat der Amerikaner, die für Moskau eh nicht akzeptabel scheint.

Kameras an: Ab 17:15 Uhr — wahrscheinlich dauert es aber eh länger — treten Merz, Macron, Burnham, Selenskyj sowie Witkoff und Kushner im Kanzleramt vor die Kameras.

PARTEIEN

SIE IST WIEDER DA: Manuela Schwesig hat sich in Berlin lange rar gemacht. Frisch im MP-Amt in Schwerin bestätigt, wird sie heute in der Hauptstadt erwartet — und jedes Wort von ihr wird darauf abgeklopft werden, was sie vorhat.

Ja, nein, vielleicht: Für den SPD-Vorsitz kandidieren? Sich Lars Klingbeil anschließen? Oder alleine? Schwesig muss bald Antworten liefern.

Etwas früh: Schwesig hätte gerne später als im Frühjahr die Parteispitze erklommen — sie steht für einen Anti-Merz-Kurs und einen möglichen Wahlkampf gegen ihn. So wird sie noch einiges von den umstrittenen Entscheidungen der Koalition mittragen müssen.

To be spotted: Heute Abend gegen 18:30 Uhr treffen sich SPD-Spitzen zum Vor-Bundesrats-Abendessen in der Hamburger Landesvertretung — eine Art erweitertes Parteipräsidium.

Nicht zu viel erwarten: In Schwesigs Umfeld wird die Bedeutung des Termins heruntergespielt, berichtet Rasmus Buchsteiner. Das Treffen sei kein Moment für Entscheidungen, sondern für Debatten darüber, welchen Kurs die SPD einschlagen werde.

BISSCHEN MÜDE NOCH: Die lange Nacht im Koalitionsausschuss steckt dem Kanzler und den anderen, die im Kanzleramt dabei waren, heute noch in den Knochen.

Unterschiedliche Interpretation: Ob das Ganze in der Nacht nun kurz vor dem Abbruch stand oder nicht, weil der Kanzler wutschnaubend seine Sachen gepackt habe — darüber gibt es aus der Runde unterschiedliche Angaben. Thorsten Frei dementiert, aber er steht damit recht allein. Viele andere bestätigen den Vorgang.

Klar: Es ging hart zur Sache im Koalitionsausschuss. Hier geht es zur Analyse von Nikolaus Doll und Rasmus.

NICHT NOCHMAL SO: Die Haushaltsberatungen für 2028 will Thorsten Frei noch vor Weihnachten starten, berichtet die Bild. „Wir werden schon auch an die Grundfesten gehen müssen.“

Für den Haushalt 2028 gebe es „Stand heute eine Deckungslücke von 25 Milliarden Euro“. Durch die Stromsteuersenkung werde sie „noch mal fünf Milliarden größer“. Für die Umsetzung aller Wünsche bräuchte es „ein jährliches Wirtschaftswachstum von vier Prozent“.

Anzeige

LÄNDERPUNKTE

WACKELIGE 2/3 MEHRHEIT? Kommenden Dienstag möchte die Berliner Linksfraktion über den Ausschluss von Vanessa Emde abstimmen. Ausgerechnet die Landesvize Martha Kleedörfer unterstützt Emde: „dass meine Partei es nicht geschafft hat, diese Antisemitismusvorwürfe gegen Vedi zurückzuweisen“ sei „ein großes Versäumnis“.

Wie weit darf man gehen? Kleedörfer findet Emdes Aussagen „legitim“. Das Leugnen des Existenzrechts Israels ist zwar nicht Parteilinie, wird aber inzwischen in der Partei geduldet, berichtet Cedric Looks. Der Parteispitze geht es vielmehr um Emdes Provokationen.

Emde-Unterstützung gab es zuletzt auch von dem Bundestagsabgeordneten Mirze Edis und dem Landesverband Bayern.

Und Emde selbst? Sie redet auf einem Kongress für einen „Sozialismus von unten“, es hängt ein Plakat mit der Aufschrift „Schluss mit dem deutschen Besatzungsterror“ und einer Wassermelone, die mutmaßlich die Auslöschung Israels darstellen soll.

JETSET

POLEN-REISE: Für Boris Pistorius geht es heute und morgen nach Krakau und Warschau. Offizieller Anlass sind Gespräche mit seinem polnischen Amtskollegen Władysław Kosiniak-Kamysz.

Mindestens genauso wichtig ist aber das Gedenken: Auf dem Programm stehen Kranzniederlegungen in Auschwitz-Birkenau, am Denkmal des Warschauer Ghettos, am Denkmal des Warschauer Aufstands und am Grabmal des Unbekannten Soldaten. Es sei dem Verteidigungsminister schon länger ein Anliegen gewesen, im Rahmen seines Amtes nach Auschwitz zu fahren, erfuhr Rixa Fürsen.

Noch gar nicht so lange her: dieser Wasserkisten-Auftritt nach der Wahl eines AfD-Landtagspräsidenten in Sachsen-Anhalt. Wer Pistorius kennt — oder wie wir beobachtet —, weiß: Das Gedenken an die Verbrechen des Nationalsozialismus und der Kampf gegen den Faschismus sind Herzensthemen des Sozialdemokraten.

Politisch relevant: das Arbeitsessen mit Kosiniak-Kamysz am Abend und die anschließende Pressekonferenz. Erst im Juni verabschiedeten beide das deutsch-polnische Verteidigungsabkommen.

Was noch folgen soll: eine Vereinbarung über eine engere Zusammenarbeit in den neuen Industrien — sprich Drohnen und Cyber. Die könnte heute finalisiert oder bald beschlossen werden.

PLENARSAALEBENE

AN KLINGBEILS HAUSHALT WIRD NOCH GESCHRAUBT: Nach der Stromsteuer ist nicht Schluss. Auch im Verkehrshaushalt wird (nach der Bereinigungssitzung!) nachverhandelt, wie Cedric erfuhr.

„Der Bund verrät seine eigene Güterbahn“ und „gefährdet Hunderttausende Jobs“, kritisiert Bahn-Gewerkschaftschef Martin Burkert nach der Bereinigungssitzung. Er spricht von einer „vollkommen unzureichenden Finanzierung“ des für den Güterverkehr zentralen Einzelwagenverkehrs. Das gefährde die DB-Tochter DB Cargo in ihrer Existenz.

Gewerkschaftsdruck wirkt: Insbesondere die SPD pocht deshalb auf eine kurzfristige Gegenleistung für die Streichung bei der Einzelwagenverkehrsförderung. In dieser Woche finden daher nochmal Verhandlungen zwischen den Verkehrshaushältern statt, um circa 100 Millionen zu finden, die es braucht.

Wo kommt das Geld her? Da man wohl nicht an andere Haushaltstitel ran möchte, ist eine kurzfristige Gegenfinanzierung über die von Patrick Schnieder im Juni ausgesetzte Richtlinie zur Trassenförderung möglich, hört Cedric.

EISENBAHN-FONDS: „Unser Ziel ist es, im nächsten Jahr einen Eisenbahn-Infrastrukturfonds für die verlässliche, langfristige und über das Sondervermögen hinaus tragbare Finanzierung der Schieneninfrastruktur zu schaffen“, sagt Steffen Bilger gegenüber Cedric. Damit kommt er der SPD-Forderung nach, den Fonds im nächsten Jahr fertigzustellen, nach.

Zur Erinnerung: Mit der Forderung nach einem „dauerhaften Sondervermögen“ für die Bahn erhöhte die SPD den Druck auf die Koalition, einen Zeitplan für den Eisenbahnkredit vorzulegen. Zugleich wollte die SPD deutlich machen, dass der Autobahnkredit nur dann kommen kann, wenn auch am Schienenkredit gearbeitet wird.

EUROVISION

RECHNEN MIT UNBEKANNTEN: „Die Angaben der Bundesregierung zur Unterstützung der Ukraine sind nicht belastbar, unvollständig und intransparent“, heißt es in diesem Bericht des Bundesrechnungshofes, der Jasper Bennink vorliegt. Bundestag und Öffentlichkeit würden dadurch nicht angemessen informiert.

Laut Bericht ermittelten die Ministerien ihre Zahlen teils manuell, auf Basis von Schätzungen oder, wie im Fall des Entwicklungsministeriums, anhand zugesagter, aber noch nicht vollständig ausgezahlter Leistungen. Das Auswärtige Amt habe für denselben Stichtag unterschiedliche Zahlen geliefert und die Abweichung laut Bericht nicht erklären können.

Unvollständig: Milliardenschwere multilaterale Leistungen über EU, UN und internationale Finanzinstitutionen würden teils gar nicht erfasst, teils als bilaterale Hilfen verbucht. Dadurch würden die Leistungen insgesamt zu niedrig ausgewiesen. Zudem tauchten bereits eingegangene Verpflichtungen für künftige Militärhilfen von mehr als zehn Milliarden Euro in der Übersicht nicht auf.

Intransparent: Kann die Ukraine EU-Darlehen nicht zurückzahlen, haftet auch Deutschland. Der BRH beziffert die Risiken aus EU-Krediten auf bis zu 42,7 Milliarden Euro. Nur 0,9 Prozent der EU-Darlehen seien über den Dotierungsfonds abgesichert.

Die Bundesregierung räumt Teile der Kritik ein und sagt Nachbesserungen zu, etwa bei Kennzeichnungen von Schätzungen oder der Darstellung von Verpflichtungsermächtigungen. Eine Gesamtsumme der Haftungsrisiken will sie weiter nicht ausweisen.

DIPLOMATISCHE DEPESCHE

KLIMA-CHINA: Neben Europa sei China das Land, das eine nachhaltige Klimapolitik global wirklich voranbringt. Das sagte der Präsident des Umweltbundesamtes (UBA), Dirk Messner, im Interview mit Johanna Sahlberg auf der Weltklimakonferenz COP31 in Antalya.

O-Ton: „China ist ökonomisch gesehen im Vergleich zu Europa mindestens ein gleichwertiger Spieler. Also das sind die beiden zentralen Akteure der globalen Klimapolitik.“

Das macht China richtig: Die Investitionen in erneuerbare Energien sind „enorm“, urteilt Messner. Beim Ausbau der Netz- und Speicherkapazitäten „müssen wir sehen, dass uns jetzt nicht die Chinesen vormachen, wie man das macht, wenn man es systematisch anbietet“.

Zwar baut China seine Kohlekraft aus: Dafür zeigt Messner aber ein gewisses Verständnis. „Die Kohle ist für die chinesische Regierung was Gas für die Europäische Union ist. Für uns ist ja Gas auch im Grunde die Übergangslösung hin zur Dekarbonisierung.“

Das gesamte Interview lesen Sie in unserem Pro Energie und Klima.

BAND DES BUNDES

TELEKOM, EIN MONOPOL? Die Monopolkommission fordert (erneut) den Verkauf der Bundesanteile an der Telekom. Die Bundesregierung erteilt dem eine Absage und will ihre Beteiligung von rund 28,6 Prozent behalten.

Sicher ist sicher: Die Beteiligung liege im „sicherheitspolitischen Interesse des Bundes” und diene dem Erhalt der digitalen Souveränität Deutschlands. Zudem warnt die Bundesregierung vor wachsenden strukturellen Abhängigkeiten bei Unterseekabeln, wie Sie in unserem Pro Technologie und KI lesen.

GESÜNDERES, KOSTENLOSES SCHULESSEN will die Vorsitzende des Gesundheitsausschusses, Tanja Machalet, mit dem anstehenden Präventionsgesetz erreichen. „Vor allem von Schulen in sozialen Brennpunkten” müssten aber auch die Eltern in die Pflicht genommen werden, so die SPD-Politikerin. Was sie sonst noch plant und was womöglich auf große Einzelhändler zukommt, lesen Sie in unserem Pro Gesundheit.

SPOTTED

PROMIS FÜR FINANZBILDUNG: Das Finanzministerium hat im Rahmen der Finanzbildungsstrategie Ex-Fußballer Philipp Lahm und die Schauspielerin Tomomi Themann als „Finanzbildungsbotschafter“ vorgestellt. Als „Brückenbauer“ sollen sie „Zielgruppen adressatengerecht und niedrigschwellig“ ansprechen — in Schulen, Vereinen oder im Netz.

Morgen geht’s los: In Pressebegleitung besuchen Klingbeil und Lahm eine Berliner Schule. Lahm und Themann arbeiten pro bono.

PREIS FÜR STUBB: Am Dienstag ist Finnlands Alexander Stubb in der Repräsentanz der Deutschen Bank in Berlin mit dem Walther-Rathenau-Preis für sein europäisches Engagement ausgezeichnet worden. Festreden hielten unter anderem Joachim Gauck und Anahita Thoms. Im Publikum saßen Friede Springer, Karsten Dreinhöfer, Dirk Niebel, Kai Sauer und viele mehr.

AGENDA

— Die Regierungspressekonferenz findet um 11:30 Uhr statt.

— Bundespräsident Frank-Walter Steinmeier besucht in Leipzig Rekruten des neuen Wehrdienstmodells bei ihrer Heimatschutzausbildung.

— Truppenbesuch: Um 9:50 Uhr ist Boris Pistorius als Festredner in Munster bei der Aufstellung acht neuer Bataillone des Heeres.

— IT-Sicherheit: Um 10 Uhr stellen Alexander Dobrindt und BSI-Chefin Claudia Plattner in der Bundespressekonferenz den BSI-Lagebericht 2026 vor.

— Digitales und Wirtschaft: Beim Handelskongress Deutschland treffen Karsten Wildberger und Katherina Reiche auf die Branche. Am Nachmittag spricht Wildberger zudem auf der BREKO-Jahrestagung über den Ausbau der digitalen Infrastruktur.

— Verkehr: In Frankfurt ist Steffen Bilger gleich doppelt gefragt: Am Morgen ist er um 9 Uhr beim Deutschen Mobilitätskongress, anschließend beim Treffen des Weimarer Dreiecks der Verkehrsminister mit seinen Amtskollegen Philippe Tabarot aus Frankreich und Dariusz Klimczak aus Polen.

— Justiz: Für Stefanie Hubig geht es nach Hamburg zur Justizministerkonferenz.

— Naturschutz: Um 17 Uhr spricht Alois Rainer im bayerischen Haibach mit dem Landesbund für Vogel- und Naturschutz.

— Europa: In Brüssel tagt der Rat „Allgemeine Angelegenheiten“. Parallel treffen sich die Bildungs- und Jugendminister der EU. Für die Bundesregierung reisen Karin Prien und Staatsminister Ronald Rauhe an.

— Bei der Weltklimakonferenz COP31 in Antalya ist Carsten Schneider weiter dabei.

— Weit, weit weg, bei den Pinguinen: In der Antarktis ist Dorothee Bär weiter mit einer wissenschaftlichen Delegation unterwegs.

ZU GUTER LETZT

SCHAUERWETTER: Der November bleibt sich auch heute treu — mit Temperaturen zwischen 6 und 10 °C, Wolken und immer wieder leichten Regenschauern. Also Regenschirm nicht vergessen!

GRUß AUS DER KÜCHE:

— Mitarbeiterrestaurant JKH: Großes Kartoffelrösti mit Kasselersteak „Hawaii“, Pfefferrahmsoße und Weißkrautsalat oder Spaghetti Bolognese mit Sonnenblumenhack

— Lampenladen PLH: Szegediner Gulasch mit Kraut und Sauerrahm, dazu Salzkartoffeln und Apfel-Karottensalat oder Kürbis-Chiasamen-Bratling an Tomaten-Risotto, dazu Kräutersoße und Rucola

— Kantine RTG: Gebratene Krakauer mit Speck-Kartoffeln, Rahm-Spitzkohl, Petersilie und Thymian oder Gemüsecurry mit Kokosmilch, Paprika, Orangensaft, Mungosprossen und Duftreis

GEBURTSTAGE: Isabelle Hemsley, Staatssekretärin im Hessischen Innenministerium (37), Wenke Brüdgam, stellvertretende Bundesvorsitzende der Linken und MdL Mecklenburg-Vorpommern (42), Michael Brand, CDU-MdB und Parlamentarischer Staatssekretär im Bildungs- und Familienministerium (53), Katarina Barley, Vizepräsidentin des EU-Parlaments (58), Jens Kraus-Massé, Botschafter im Tschad (65)

🗞️ Happiness is a bowl of borscht

19 November 2026 | Daily newsletter

Food at the front

GTA VI

Smoked out

Good morning,

Where do you go out to eat in a war zone? In today's top story, our Ukraine correspondent takes us on a food tour along the front line and explains why being able to order a beer with your lunch in Kramatorsk is a bad sign. We also look at where smoke-flavoured snacks went and have the math on how much of your monthly salary it takes to afford GTA VI.

Toyah Höher

Editor

Food

The last good meal before the front

A culinary journey through Ukraine at war, one meal at a time.

〉 Read article 〉 Hide again

Joseph Roche

A warm bowl of borscht in a cold country, after a long day of work. Maybe that's what happiness is all about.

I'm sitting in Trypichchia, a traditional restaurant in Kharkiv, a city about 30 km from Russian positions.

And this borscht, I swear to god, might be the best I've ever had in my entire life. As a devoted enthusiast, I've eaten it in every possible setting: in fancy restaurants, at petrol stations, in village canteens, in shelters, and in trenches. I know my borscht.

Mykyta, 29, one of the founders, tells us that the place started out as a local canteen at the beginning of Russia's full-scale invasion. Its sole purpose was to feed soldiers and volunteers who had stayed in the city when Russian forces were on the verge of capturing it.

Since then, it has grown into a 300-sq-metre restaurant dedicated to one thing: “Serving the best food at the lowest price while rediscovering Ukrainian cuisine in a Kharkiv that has been Russified for far too long.”

And you can feel it.

Every recipe, Mykyta explains, is quite complex.

The borscht is made with beet “kvass” (fermented beetroot juice), which gives it a lovely acidic kick and an even deeper reddish colour. That's the difference between an OK borscht and something worth driving into a war zone for.

When Trypichchia is closed, the other option is Taco Loco, a Mexican restaurant opened by a Colombian-American long before the full-scale invasion. A Mexican might never call this Mexican food, but hear me out. We're 30 km from Russian troops, and their margaritas are damn good.

It also happens to serve some of the best tacos I've had – in Ukraine, maybe not in the world. Let's not get carried away.

The owner himself is now serving in the army. He doesn't seem particularly keen to talk about it, but we're not here for that anyway.

I'm much more interested in his taco recipe.

“My mum's recipe,” he says. A good marinade with onions, lemon juice, paprika, cumin, and so on. But, as he also points out, Ukrainian produce is among the best he's ever had.

“Especially compared with what we have in the US,” he says. “Here, a tomato tastes like a tomato, and a cucumber tastes like a cucumber.”

You might think these are the last decent meals before the Donbas, where nothing but greasy kebabs and triangular sandwiches awaits. Well, you'd be surprised. In Izium, somewhere between military shops and half-destroyed buildings, you can have one of the most exquisite culinary experiences of your life in a car park.

The place is run by Zhenya. I'm not even sure it has a name, but it honestly doesn't need one. Soldiers know where to find him when they’re hungry and craving something simple but, above all, delicious.

Zhenya cooks his chicken for hours over glowing charcoal before cutting it into generous chunks and piling them onto a paper plate. If you ask, he'll smother it in his homemade barbecue sauce.

“With all the soldiers around, business is actually doing pretty well,” he tells us during his break. “It all comes down to my two-day marinade.”

What's in the marinade, I dare to ask.

He laughs, lights his cigarette, and waves a finger at me. “Even the Russians, during the occupation of the city [in 2022], couldn't get my recipe.”

Fair enough.

After a good lunch, we need a decent coffee. Let's head to Makers Coffee, a trendy coffee shop in Izium that has become something of a headquarters for me over the years.

In summer, my usual order is an espresso tonic: tonic water, plenty of ice, and a shot of espresso. Granted, there's nothing Ukrainian about it. It was invented by a Norwegian barista in 2007. But it's actually rather good.

The best part about Makers is that waiters don't get angry when you dump all your equipment on the floor and stay for five hours, waiting for a press officer to grant you access somewhere.

The Donbas used to have its share of excellent places to eat, too. I could tell you about restaurants in Dobropillia, Pokrovsk, or Chasiv Yar. They're all gone due to the heavy fighting in the region.

As I write this, I've just seen that Golden Cup, a cool little café in Sloviansk that I used to visit, has been blown up. They had great quiche. My favourite burger joint, just down the street, is gone too.

I now think about these places with nostalgia. Whenever I'm on assignment, I try to make the most of them, knowing it might be the last time I get to eat there.

That's exactly how I felt in Kramatorsk in October. One of the last remaining cities in the Donbas under Ukrainian control, it's being reduced to rubble, with drones constantly hovering overhead.

I passed by the first restaurant I ever ate at in the city, back in 2022. Gone. Black Bar and The Pub, gone too.

I eventually found a small canteen. No sign above the entrance. They were serving Ukrainian food such as borscht, “varenyky” (filled dumplings), or “holubtsi” (stuffed cabbage rolls). I was feeling a bit nervous that day and not particularly hungry, so I just ordered a plate of “deruny” (small fried potato pancakes).

The place was even serving alcohol. In the Donbas, this is forbidden under martial law. I ordered a beer.

“That's a sign the city is about to fall,” one of my friends joked. “That, and the contraband cigarettes.”

I laughed. A bitter laugh.

Outside, soldiers with wild eyes had just finished their meals and were heading out for a cigarette, their guns at the ready in case they spotted any drones.

Then came a boom, followed by another. Something had landed nearby.

I wouldn't be ordering dessert that day. We needed to wrap things up as quickly as possible and leave before sundown.

All I could think about was getting back to Kharkiv, sitting down at Trypichchia, ordering another beer, and, of course, another bowl of beet-kvass borscht. It tasted even better than the last one.

Grand Theft Wage

Grand Theft Auto VI is out today. It's the most anticipated video game of the decade (the last GTA came out in 2013), reportedly one of the most expensive ever made, and potentially one of the most profitable. Some predictions suggest it could bring in up to USD 5 billion in global sales in its first week alone.

Europe is a massive market for GTA. The game costs around €80 in most countries, but its affordability varies once you factor in purchasing power. A familiar pattern in globalised products, like a Netflix subscription. For both, Ukrainians get the worst deal.

The hype over the past few days has been insane. Gaming is a world of its own, but GTA is one of those rare franchises that breaks out of that bubble and gets everyone talking, including the mainstream media. Some viral headlines have even warned of a productivity drop as employees call in sick to play, something dubbed “GTA Flu”.

But as The Guardian points out, GTA Flu seems to be more of a media phenomenon than an actual economic crisis. Still, the fact that we're even talking about it says something about the scale of this cultural moment.

Nathan Domon and Sebastian Gräff

Food flavourings

Here, have some cancer with your smoky bacon crisps

Aoife White

The taste of smoke triggers memories of cosy firesides and tasty barbecues. Think smoked ham, smoked salmon, smoked cheese, and the less traditional smoky bacon crisps.

Smoke flavourings are usually made by burning wood, capturing the smoke, and turning it into a liquid that can be added to food.

But these smoky flavours may damage DNA and risk causing cancer, EU food experts said in 2023, leading to an EU ban on eight substances that came into effect in July for flavours added to sauces, soups, and snacks.

And more are now set to be snuffed out: a wider ban on smoke flavourings in ham, fish, and cheese will land in 2029. The traditional method of exposing food to smoke and heat in a smokehouse oven, though it too can introduce some toxic compounds, is still allowed.

The flavourings industry has tried, and failed, to fight back. Food flavourings companies Kerry Inc and Kerry Ingredients last week lost their legal fight to overturn the ban for three flavours they make.

Kerry and other manufacturers have been trying to find smoky alternatives or evoke smokiness with herbs, spices, or salt, with limited success. One company talks about “rebuilding flavour profiles layer by layer to recreate not only smokiness, but also aroma, depth and mouthfeel.” Sounds like a lot of engineering.

Snack fans aren't always impressed. Portuguese and British crisp lovers complain that their favourites just don't taste the same as before, or are harder to find.

The EU threat to smoky bacon-flavoured crisps has raised some hackles in the UK, which is currently trying to strike a deal to ease the trade of dairy and meat products with the EU. Despite having left the EU, the UK will most likely have to accept its rules on food safety as part of that deal.

For the past 30 years, British tabloid newspapers have loved spreading “Euromyths” about EU food rules, including the “barmy Brussels ban” on bendy bananas, an infamous EU ban on banana curvature that never actually existed. Those reports fuelled euroscepticism.

Lovers of any smoked cheese, sausage, or fish using smoky flavourings, beware. Your recipes may be about to change.

Last but not least

If you've ever played GTA, you know that music is a big part of the experience. The game features several radio stations packed with licensed songs from artists across genres. But there's also original music, and for GTA VI, the original score was composed by French electronic duo Justice (you probably know this 2000s classic from them).

The duo spent three years on the project. They already released the track Flower in a Hurricane (featuring Tame Impala, SZA, King Gizzard & the Lizard Wizard), which was used in the game's launch trailer. It's got a fun, retro-futuristic vibe, with a cool '80s guitar riff, plenty of synths, and that classic French electro sound.

Justice composed 50 songs for the game, totalling three hours of original music. The album is due out on 11 December.

Nathan Domon

Flower In A Hurricane on Spotify

GTA IV Orignial Score on Spotify

German employees in 12 states don't even have to call in sick to play GTA VI: they could request educational leave for a three-day course analysing “open-world” games. We got paid time off to play video games before GTA VI. And with that, the meme can die.

Toyah Höher

Digitale Welt: Wie sicher ist die IT-Infrastruktur? (Foto: Moment/Getty Images)

Guten Morgen, liebe Leserin, lieber Leser,in der Konfliktforschung gibt es ein großes Angstszenario: Ein Gegner zermürbt eine Gesellschaft mit unzahligen kleinen Sabotageakten – so lange, bis eine relevante Zahl an Menschen sagt: „Hier funktioniert nichts mehr“, und den eigenen Staat infrage stellt. Bisher dachte man, solch einen hybriden Krieg konnten nur feindliche Regime heraufbeschworen.

Das war, bevor Künstliche Intelligenz (KI) immer leistungsfahiger wurde.

Wie unter dem Brennglas lasst sich gerade in vielen westlichen Staaten beobachten, wie sich ein Szenario unzahliger Alltagspannen mit unbekanntem Verursacher anfühlt: Binnen einer Woche fielen in den USA die Flugsicherung, Microsofts Bürosoftware, Systeme bei Chase und Apple und ein internes Netz des Geheimdienstes NSA aus. In Europa heizten Supermarktkühltruhen anstatt zu kühlen, die Universitaten Leipzig und Tübingen wurden Opfer von Hackern. Und weltweit sorgte gestern eine Warnung, die Programmiersprache Java biete ein Einfallstor für Hacker, für Unruhe. Ein Forscher hatte die Sicherheitslücke mit OpenAIs Codex gefunden – in rund einer Stunde.

Es gibt keine Hinweise darauf, dass diese Vorfalle orchestriert sind: hier veraltete Systeme, dort Hackerangriffe, wieder woanders Sicherheitslücken. Was diese Vorfalle verbindet: Sie sind oftmals auf die atemberaubenden Fortschritte der KI und deren Potenzial, bisherige IT-Sicherheitskonzepte zu unterlaufen, zurückzuführen.

Weil KI Lücken schneller findet als je zuvor, flicken Unternehmen im Akkord: Allein Microsoft schloss im Oktober 1400 Sicherheitslücken, ein Jahr zuvor waren es 170. Dieses Tempo überlaste viele Systeme, glaubt US-Senator Mark Warner, Vize-Chef des Geheimdienstausschusses. Selbst ein Regierungsvertreter führt die Ausfalle inzwischen auf Updates und Patches zurück. Die Prasidentin der deutschen IT-Sicherheitsbehorde BSI, Claudia Plattner, spricht von einer „neuen Zeitrechnung der Cybersicherheit“.

Und wahrend US-Prasident Donald Trump noch sagte, solche Dinge „passieren halt“, sagte sein Vize J.D. Vance gestern kurzfristig offentliche Termine ab, um an Krisensitzungen teilzunehmen.

Was bleibt: Das Gefühl, eine hybride Bedrohung lege den Alltag lahm, kann mittlerweile jeder auslosen. Unser Technologie-Chef Stephan Scheuer bringt es auf den Punkt:

Die Zeit des freien Internets ist am Ende.

Anthropic-Chef Dario Amodei: Plotzlich Milliardar (Foto: Bloomberg)

Anthropic: Der großte Borsengang aller Zeiten?

Ungeachtet der Zweifel an den fundamentalen Daten der großen KI-Konzerne und den Auswirkungen der Technologie, dürfte KI-Pionier Anthropic heute den großten Borsengang aller Zeiten hinlegen. Die Aktie des Unternehmens, dessen Sprachmodell Claude derzeit beim Publikum das beliebteste der Welt ist, soll nach Vorstellungen des Unternehmens heute mit einem Preis von 83 Dollar erstmals in den Handel an der US-Technologieborse Nasdaq starten. Zuvor lag das obere Ende der avisierten Preisspanne bei 78 Euro. Zudem erhohte Anthropic das Volumen des Angebots. Damit dürfte der Konzern durch den Borsengang knapp 95 Milliarden Dollar erlosen und ware an der Borse etwa 1,5 Billionen Dollar Wert.

Großter Gewinner werden heute aber wohl weder Anleger noch Anthropic sein – sondern das Gros der Wagniskapitalgeber. Profitieren dürften vor allem die Lieferanten des Start-ups: Die großten sind Amazon und Google.

Parallel zur Emission verkauft Anthropic für 26 Milliarden Dollar weitere stimmrechtslose Aktien an sieben Technologiekonzerne, und zwar zum Ausgabepreis: Chipentwickler Nvidia, Google, die Chiphersteller AMD, Broadcom und Micron sowie Microsoft und der taiwanesische Auftragsfertiger TSMC. Das Geld dürfte zu wesentlichen Teilen an die Lieferanten zurückfließen. Für den Mega-Borsengang heute gilt für die gesamte KI-Okonomie: Neben Faszination und Wetten auf die Zukunft pragt vor allem eine fortgesetzte Kreislaufwirtschaft den Wert der Unternehmen.

Der Kanzler verlasst das Kanzleramt: Wenig Wirkung, hoher Preis (Foto: Christoph Gateau/dpa)

Regierung: Mit dem Kanzlerkopf durch die Wand

Die Bundesregierung hat sich also doch noch auf die Senkung der Stromsteuer geeinigt. Erkauft hat sie der Kanzler zu einem hohen Preis: Friedrich Merz (CDU) musste der SPD den ordnungspolitisch fragwürdigen Preisdeckel auf Sprit versprechen. Und er befeuerte Zweifel an seinen Führungsfahigkeiten, weil er nach Angaben von Teilnehmern zu fortgeschrittener Stunde des Koalitionsausschusses genervt den Raum verließ. Und das alles für eine durchschnittliche jahrliche Entlastung von 80 Euro pro Haushalt. Was in der Emporung über den Vorgang gestern allerdings unterging: Viele Unternehmen profitieren mit fünf- oder sechsstelligen Summen.

Für private Steuerzahler dagegen fallt die Gesamtentlastung im kommenden Jahr überschaubar aus. Das IW Koln hat berechnet, wie sich alle steuerpolitischen Beschlüsse der Regierung auswirken. Eine Familie mit zwei Kindern kann somit etwa 552 Euro mehr als dieses Jahr verplanen, Haushalte ohne Kinder zwischen 150 und 250 Euro. Wobei nach dem mitternachtlichen Fluchtversuch des Kanzlers aus den Koalitionsgesprachen noch eine Frage offen ist: Wie sehr ein Haushalt entlastet wird, in dem kein Kind, dafür aber ein Kindskopf lebt.

Geopolitik: Zwei Gipfel, ein Zeitalter

Heute finden zwei Gipfel statt, die unterschiedlicher kaum sein konnten. Im chinesischen Shenzhen trifft Gastgeber Xi Jinping am Rande des Apec-Gipfels erstmals in einer Dreierrunde auf Donald Trump und Wladimir Putin. Für Putin ein Ritterschlag, sagt der Kolner Politologe Thomas Jager: „Putin wird sich dann als dritte Weltmacht fühlen.“

Zeitgleich empfangt Merz mehr als 20 Regierungschefs der Ukraine-Unterstützer im Kanzleramt. So befremdlich die Bilder aus Shenzhen auch sind, wo der Prasident der USA mit zwei Despoten kumpelt: Im Vergleich zu den Fotos aus Berlin zeigen sie so eindrucksvoll wie selten, dass das pazifische Zeitalter langst begonnen hat.

Auto: Das doppelte China-Problem von Mercedes

Mercedes plagt sich gleich mit zwei China-Problemen herum. Wie alle deutschen Autohersteller ignorierte auch das Mercedes-Management über Jahre die Mahnungen, sich nicht zu stark von China abhangig zu machen. Das racht sich, das Geschaft dort erodiert. Das Wachstum in den USA soll dies ausgleichen. Und da beginnt das zweite China-Problem.

Ein Gesetzentwurf im US-Senat würde Autobauern den Verkauf vernetzter Autos faktisch verbieten, wenn Chinesen mehr als 15 Prozent an ihnen halten. Bei Mercedes sind es fast 20 Prozent: Der Staatskonzern BAIC halt 9,98 Prozent, Geely-Gründer Li Shufu 9,69 Prozent. Die ranghochsten Mitglieder im China-Ausschuss des Reprasentantenhauses verlangen nun bis 1. Dezember umfangreiche Unterlagen. Der Ton ist kernig: Mercedes stelle sich „aktiv“ gegen Gesetze. Eine Losung gabe es: Vor einem Verbot würde Mercedes die chinesischen Aktionare unter der Schwelle herauskaufen, sagt ein Topmanager. Und eins hat der Konzern schon erreicht: Der Brief tragt die Unterschriften eines Republikaners und eines Demokraten. Das schafft in Washington derzeit kaum jemand.

Paketdienste: DPD und GLS wollen gemeinsame Sache machen

Paketlieferungen sind wie Papiertaschentücher: Produkt und großter Anbieter sind für mich eins. Wahrend ich Papiertaschentücher konsequent „Tempos“ nenne, bringt die Pakete DHL. Darüber ist ein wenig in Vergessenheit geraten, dass es auch andere Anbieter gibt. Was die nun offenbar stort: DPD und GLS wollen ihr Deutschlandgeschaft zusammenlegen. Gemeinsam kommen beide auf 20 Prozent Marktanteil. Stimmt das Kartellamt zu, hielte GLS 80 Prozent am Gemeinschaftsunternehmen.

Bemerkenswert ist die Konstellation: Die Paketdienste der franzosischen und der britischen Post greifen die Deutsche Post an – und im Hintergrund wirkt ein tschechischer Milliardar mit, GLS-Eigentümer Daniel Křetinsky. Europaischer Binnenmarkt, wie er im Buche steht.

Philipp Lahm zu aktiven Zeiten: Gewinne mitnehmen (Foto: dpa)

Philipp Lahm: Verdienen wie ein Fußballprofi

Zum Schluss schauen wir auf Fußball-Legende Philipp Lahm. Der Weltmeister soll dem Nachwuchs künftig Finanzen statt Fußball beibringen. Lahm wird dafür Botschafter der vom Bundeskabinett beschlossenen Finanzbildungsstrategie. Die wichtigste Finanzlektion hat Lahm ohnehin schon 2014 erteilt: Nach dem WM-Titel trat er aus der Nationalmannschaft zurück. Gewinne mitnehmen, wenn der Kurs am hochsten steht – mehr Finanzbildung geht kaum.

Ich wünsche Ihnen einen Donnerstag mit lauter Hochststanden.

Snapshot of the day

November 18, 2026

Anirudh S.K., Kalrav Joshi

An encounter took place in Kashmir’s Kulgam this morning, following which security forces identified the deceased as 22-year-old Mohammad Lateef Bhat, whom they said was the Lashkar-e-Taiba terrorist outfit’s last active local commander in the valley. The authorities have said that Bhat and Umar Dar – who was slain in a previous encounter on Monday – were involved in the terror attack on a Central Police Reserve Force base in Kulgam last week wherein three jawans were wounded. Bhat’s death, writes Junaid Dar, is expected to bring to a close the over-seven-day-long intensive cordon-and-search operations in Kulgam. Security personnel have restricted civilian movement, frisked locals frequently and, reportedly, even made people stand outdoors amid the winter cold. Kashmir’s politicians raised the alarm yesterday saying these operations are inflicting a collective punishment on civilians for a crime they did not commit.

In the ‘mother of democracy’, local elections appear to be turning into an increasingly distant prospect. Despite an Allahabad high court order last month directing the state government and the Uttar Pradesh state election commission to complete the panchayat polls within three months, the BJP-led state government has approved an ordinance postponing elections across all 57,694 gram panchayats by another six months. The delay makes it likely that the polls will be held after the 2027 assembly elections, potentially by May 2027. The tenure of the OBC commission has also been extended.

The Supreme Court has declined to immediately stay the interim bail granted to senior Samajwadi Party leader Azam Khan by the Allahabad high court, observing that “heavens will not fall” if the former Uttar Pradesh minister is allowed to remain on bail. The remarks came after the Enforcement Directorate challenged the high court’s decision before the apex court. Earlier, the high court on Tuesday had granted Khan interim bail until December 10, observing that the circumstances surrounding the ED’s case and his arrest clearly pointed to the “motivated and malafide nature” of the proceedings.

When the Supreme Court said that the Delhi police must not prevent lawyers, journalists and other professionals from doing their jobs during the protests demanding the chief election commissioner’s resignation, surely that direction did not apply to “so-called reel makers and social media influencers”, the cops have submitted before the bench. With so many such individuals covering the protests the police had a hard time telling them apart from real journalists, they added.

Notwithstanding the fact that press cards did not prevent journalists from being detained or nearly detained during the protests anyway, many independent reporters have pointed out that just because they lack accreditation it cannot mean that their work – including making reels – does not constitute journalism. And ‘if the police genuinely found it difficult to distinguish between independent journalists and social media influencers, they should seek a clearer mechanism rather than dismissing an entire category of reporters’, independent journalist Kadambini Sharma pointed out speaking to The Hindu‘s Lavpreet Kaur.

After Donald Trump took over as president in January 2025 the Quad’s leaders skipped a full year before meeting yesterday in Manila, and the outcome of their meeting was different in more than one significant way from the last summit held in Delaware. Devirupa Mitra ...

The Upgrade Apocalypse

Plus: Nvidia beats expectations. Meet your new Democratic leaders. Why is Hegseth in Venezuela? And a new discovery reshapes the history of cannabis.

Jessica Yellin and Rohan Montgomery

Nov 18

READ IN APP

Trump shakes hands with Vladimir Putin as Xi Jinping looks on. The leaders are gathered in Shenzhen, China, for the APEC summit. (Photo by Iori Sagisawa / POOL / AFP via Getty Images)

For daily news, updates, and analysis, be sure to follow us on Instagram. If you are able to support independent journalism, please make a tax-deductible donation to News Not Noise here.

Here’s what I’m hearing about this week’s national technology freakout from my bench of national security, intelligence, and cybersecurity sources. None of them has any interest in defending this administration. They tell me we’re witnessing an upgrade apocalypse.

The rush to AI is overwhelming aging infrastructure. Some call it Y2K, 26 years late. AI skeptics warned we’d eventually suffer failures serious enough to force safeguards. Maybe we’ve arrived.

What about a cyberattack? A few dissenters think a hostile actor is sending a warning. One veteran national security official scoffed that if this were an attack, “we didn’t even sneeze.” He told me to stand down on the conspiracy theories.

Could the administration be concealing an attack to prevent panic? Sure. But the director of national intelligence denied it under oath today, and lying to Congress risks prison. (Yes, Trump could pardon him.)

I trust my sources. But we’re left to piece together what’s happening because the people in charge aren’t giving substantive answers, don’t seem to understand the problem themselves, and can’t even manage a convincing show of competence.

On the failure of leadership, at least, the intelligence is unanimous.

Yesterday I spoke with former CIA analyst Julia Curlee about what may have caused the FAA, NSA, and bank outages, whether they’re connected, and where AI fits in. You can find that here:

News Not Noise is a reader-supported publication. To receive exclusive content and support our work, please consider becoming a paid subscriber.

Upgrade to paid

Here Are Your Headlines

Everything’s Breaking: The wave of tech outages continues. The National Security Agency’s classified internal network, NSANet, went down for hours after workers patched newly discovered vulnerabilities. Apple Pay, iCloud, and other Apple services briefly failed after an internal update. That follows outages at Microsoft, the FAA, Workday, United Airlines, and JPMorgan Chase, all blamed on unspecified technical issues or software bugs, often right after an update or upgrade. Technical glitches happen all the time, and there’s no evidence these are connected. But so many, hitting such critical systems in quick succession, strikes many experts as suspicious. What’s going on? There are two main theories, and both may be true:

Information Overload: The first is that organizations can’t keep up with how complex modern software has become, or how fast it’s changing. Most developers now use AI tools that write code faster than humans can review it, and that code is often too complex for many to understand. One expert described the result as “a highly complex system made of low-quality parts, where a single error can compromise everything.” AI also makes it easier for bad actors to find and exploit vulnerabilities. That forces organizations to rush out defensive patches, sometimes onto aging systems that buckle under the load. NSANet is a case in point: Director of National Intelligence Jay Clayton said it failed after an update meant to fix a key vulnerability that was discovered with AI’s help weeks earlier.

Hacker Paradise: The second theory is cyberattacks. The Trump administration says there’s no evidence of any, but some experts say they can’t rule it out. AI is making attacks easier, more frequent, and possible in ways humans alone couldn’t manage; one expert said the “threat is worse than it’s ever been.” The day the FAA grounded flights, the FBI warned that bad actors had obtained an AI-assisted tool organizations use to find holes in their own systems. Since then:

Researchers disclosed a flaw in Java, one of the world’s most widely used programming languages, that could expose sensitive data or let attackers run malicious code.

Attackers hit 178 organizations through a popular third-party tool, trying to steal crypto and card details.

Google said Russian-language hackers carried out what it called the first cyberattack fully automated by AI, with no human involvement.

Invest In Defense: Whatever is behind the outages, experts broadly agree organizations need to invest more in cybersecurity.

What You Can Do: Scammers will try to exploit the confusion, for example with a phishing email claiming your bank was hacked and asking you to call. Don’t engage with suspicious messages. If you’re worried, contact your bank, employer, or whoever is supposedly involved directly. Keep your devices updated and your passwords strong.

Share

Not Enough: Nvidia beat expectations on revenue and earnings, including its own. That didn’t ease worries about its future without co-founder and former CEO Jensen Huang, and its stock kept sliding after a brief rally. Some investors and employees are still pushing for Huang’s return, but the board reiterated that won’t happen. Interim CEO Colette Kress told employees at an all-hands meeting to “remember, we’ve got this.”

Shifting Sands: Investors may also be uneasy about signs Nvidia is retreating from Huang’s more controversial moneymakers, like aggressively financing its own customers and pushing to sell chips to China. Nvidia said it will stop selling its H200 chips to China, exiting a deal that gave the U.S. government a 25% cut of those sales. It also created a National Security and Export Control Oversight Committee, which some see as a bid to convince lawmakers it’s taking national security seriously.

Conflict of Interest: Senior Democrats are investigating whether Commerce Secretary Howard Lutnick’s alleged obstruction of action against Megaspeed, the company accused of smuggling Nvidia chips into China, was influenced by his family firm. Cantor Fitzgerald held hundreds of millions of dollars in Nvidia stock. “Secretary Lutnick’s reported obstruction may have resulted in billions of dollars of restricted AI chips being diverted to China,” they wrote. “It also propped up the prices of NVIDIA for months, preventing devastating losses for” Cantor Fitzgerald. The company has cut its Nvidia holdings almost in half since Lutnick joined the administration, but has kept promoting the stock.

Historic Meeting: Trump arrived in Shenzhen, China, where Xi Jinping greeted him on the tarmac, returning the gesture Trump made earlier this year. The two leaders even hugged. Trump, Xi, and Putin will hold a brief three-way meeting tomorrow, and Trump will meet each separately. Talks are expected to focus on nuclear arms control and the war in Ukraine. Experts don’t expect major deals.

Ad Libber in Manila: Trump claimed a “very big trade deal” with the Philippines. He offered no details and the Philippines hasn’t mentioned one.

Smooth Sailing: House Democrats formally nominated Rep. Hakeem Jeffries (D-NY) for speaker, putting him on track to become the first Black speaker of the House when the new Congress convenes in January. Despite some opposition on the left, Jeffries ran unopposed and won the caucus vote 251–11. He’ll lead the largest Democratic House majority in 35 years.

Other Firsts: Jeffries isn’t the only Democratic leader making history. Rep. Katherine Clark (D-MA) will become the first woman House majority leader, Rep. Pete Aguilar (D-CA) the first Latino majority whip, and Rep. Ted Lieu (D-CA) the first Asian American chair of the House Democratic Caucus.

Share

Surprise Trip: Defense Secretary Pete Hegseth made an unannounced visit to Venezuela, where he boasted about the capture of Nicolás Maduro and announced a military agreement with the former U.S. adversary that reportedly includes military reforms and training. Hegseth praised Venezuela as a “compliant security partner” and vowed to hunt down and kill “narco-terrorists.” Some experts see the trip as a warning to Venezuelan leaders not to resist what one Venezuelan journalist called the Trump administration’s “direct administration” of the country. Trump was even blunter today, calling Venezuela an “acquisition, whether people like to say that or not.”

Friends in High Places: Hegseth also met with Alejandro Betancourt, the oil magnate at the center of a controversial deal to extract Venezuela’s oil and send it, along with much of the profit, to the U.S. Catch up on that here.

New Frontier: Widespread anxiety about the sustainability of the AI boom hasn’t dampened excitement around Anthropic’s IPO, which is set for tomorrow. It’ll debut on the Nasdaq stock exchange under the symbol ANT, reportedly for $83 a share. That would result in one of the biggest IPOs in history.

Missing Ingredient: The White House withdrew its nomination of Heidi Overton for FDA commissioner, blaming a lack of support among Republicans. Some were frustrated she refused to commit to banning mail deliveries of mifepristone, a key abortion medication which she has argued should be heavily restricted. Sen. Bill Cassidy (R-LA) claimed the administration withdrew Overton’s nomination rather than make concrete commitments to anti-abortion senators. Other lawmakers questioned Overton’s independence from certain Trump administration policies, like breaking up vaccines and allowing flavored vapes.

Some Dry Season: Parts of central and south Florida are under a flood watch, with some areas expected to get up to 18 inches of rain through Friday. The super El Niño is disrupting what is normally Florida’s dry season. On the other side of the country, officials issued evacuation orders and closed beaches and roads as massive waves, some over 50ft, hit California’s coast. Two waterspouts appeared in San Francisco Bay. The risk of coastal flooding remains elevated through Thursday, according to the National Weather Service. Stay safe!

Upgrade to paid

News That Doesn’t Suck

Smoking Gun: It’s been 30 years since the first U.S. state legalized cannabis. Today, more people consume it daily than any other intoxicant, including alcohol. But our relationship with Mary Jane goes back farther than you might think — as researchers just discovered. Archeologists were excavating an Iron Age tomb in Siberia when they spotted what turned out to be hundreds of cannabis seeds. It’s extremely rare for plant matter to be preserved like this, so that was already a major find. But then the researchers also found human hair, which one said was “almost too good to be true.” Why? Because they could use the hair to conduct a drug test — which came back positive for THC, the psychoactive compound in cannabis that makes you high. Radiocarbon dating showed that the seeds were left in the tomb around 2,800 years ago, making this the earliest evidence of humans consuming cannabis specifically for its intoxicating effects. Researchers say this discovery will reshape our understanding of our historical relationship with cannabis — and potentially modern attitudes toward it, too.

What A Day: Hack to the Future

The latest word on AI and the outages.

Matt Berg

Nov 18

READ IN APP

X MARKS THE BOT

Is AI behind the widespread outages? Trump’s team and experts are floating a tentative new answer: Sort of, but not quite in the way that you think.

After a week of massive outages at companies and government agencies that began around Friday the 13th (guys, we should have known!), President Donald Trump’s team has a new explanation for what’s been going on. They still insist there’s no evidence of a widespread hacking campaign, or an artificial intelligence-powered attack. But AI still might have played a role, according to Secretary of State Marco Rubio — or, rather, the reaction to it may have.

The outages could be linked to IT teams rushing to respond to the hacking threat posed by the rise of AI, as organizations rapidly patch their systems with upgrades that spark their own temporary turmoil, Rubio told reporters.

“Sometimes … it creates a short-term disruption in the way your system works,” Rubio said. “That’s how that’s how it’s been described to me, in terms of the role that [AI] might have played.”

This theory was echoed by Sen. Mark Warner (D-VA) and other cybersecurity experts. These problems should be a wake-up call for Congress to regulate artificial intelligence, Warner tweeted.

These outages also raise another pressing question: Is America ready for potential AI-powered attacks in the future? Director of National Intelligence Jay Clayton didn’t sound too confident this morning. “Superintelligence is sharply increasing speed, scale, and sophistication of offensive and defensive cyber operations,” he told lawmakers.

The Trump administration’s fumbling response and garbled public messaging is also causing plenty of alarm.

In the absence of clear public explanations, the problems at Microsoft, the FAA, JPMorgan Chase, Apple and the National Security Agency are still prompting fear, questions and conspiracy theories. They’re also making life awkward for top Trump officials, who are clearly not on top of the situation.

DHS Secretary Markwayne Mullin caught heat this week after news broke that he flew to a college football game in Louisiana over the weekend, even as passengers across the country were stranded due to the nationwide airplane ground stop. He fiercely defended himself in front of Congress this morning… with a peculiar argument: I love my family!

“I took my family and my great nieces to an LSU game that was scheduled for weeks prior to that because I wanted to be a good uncle and take my little niece, who has never been to an LSU game, and she’s a huge LSU fan,” Mullin said, noting that he had other meetings in the state planned as well.

No one, of course, is suggesting that the solution to this crisis is for Markwayne Mullin to be a bad uncle. It would be cool, however, if the head of homeland security were a bit more focused on, y’know, homeland security, rather than football.

FAA Administrator Bryan Bedford took responsibility for the ground stop today, urging people to stop bashing Transportation Secretary Sean Duffy. “I’m the guy they hired to get this done. So blame me if we need to blame somebody,” Bedford said at an event with lawmakers and aviation officials.

Enough with the football games and finger-pointing. Can someone just figure out what actually happened?!

WHAT ELSE? 👀

House Democrats nominated Hakeem Jeffries to be the next speaker, which would make him the first Black lawmaker to hold the position. The full House is expected to formally elect him to the post in January, when Dems seize the majority.

Donald Trump shook hands with Russian dictator Vladimir Putin and hugged Chinese President Xi Jinping during his trip to China today. Trump is expected to meet separately with both leaders tomorrow, in addition to a trilateral meeting with them to discuss the Russia-Ukraine war. Nothing like a good hang with the homies!

Democrat Mary Peltola defeated Sen. Dan Sullivan (R-AK), marking the first time in 18 years that a Democrat has been elected to the Senate from The Last Frontier. Senate Dems now have a 56-seat majority. Trump’s Department of Justice, however, said that it still plans to probe Peltola’s campaign to see if there was an intentional effort to confuse voters with the “spoiler” Dan Sullivan candidate.

Trump has grown increasingly frustrated with JD Vance over the veep’s criticism of the Iran war following the GOP’s defeat in the midterms, the New York Times writes. Did anyone really think Trump would stay chill about this? Meanwhile, Trump has been privately praising Marco Rubio, saying that he could make a formidable presidential candidate.

Rep. Robert Garcia (D-CA), the soon-to-be chair of the House Oversight Committee, sent letters to high-profile Trump operatives, directing them to preserve documents in case they’re investigated by Democrats. His initial target list includes: Don Jr., Eric Trump, Stephen Miller, Susie Wiles, JD Vance, Jared Kushner, Todd Blanche, Kimberly Guilfoyle, Kristi Noem, Corey Lewandowski, and two federal prison officials associated with Ghislaine Maxwell’s transfer to a minimum-security prison.

The White House pulled Heidi Overton, its nominee to lead the FDA, due to a lack of support in the Senate. Sen. Bill Cassidy (R-LA) described the decision to pull her as “odd.” He wrote: “I was having productive conversations with members. I believe she would have had the votes to pass out of committee and pass the full Senate.”

The majority of Americans believe a Democrat will be elected president in 2028, according to a new poll. Only 28 percent think a Republican will win, and 20 percent said they don’t know. Here’s an interesting take from a local GOP chair in Michigan: “As much as I like Rubio, and as much as I like Vance, they can’t be our nominee,” he told Politico. “We need to get a Republican as far away from Trump as possible, and even then, I think it’s going to be a battle.”

American federal prosecutors charged an Irish man for allegedly destroying a $60 million U.S. military plane in Ireland in April. “He allegedly broke into the aircraft, cut critical wires, contaminated fuel tanks, destroyed gauges and poured corrosive substances onto the aircraft’s components,” the Washington Post writes. Wow!

LIGHT AT THE END… ☀️

NASA’s ​Voyager 1 probe is estimated to be one light day from Earth, 49 years after it was launched. That’s 16 billion miles! The spacecraft is expected to ping NASA within a (human) day, confirming its distance. “Reaching one light-day is an astounding feat, one that I never expected to see,” Voyager project ​manager Suzanne Dodd told Reuters.

The long-endangered San Francisco garter snake is making a comeback. Scientists recently released 62 snakes into the wild after raising them in a zoo, as part of new conservation efforts. The snakes, known as “one of the most beautiful snakes” on the continent, have been illegally hunted by collectors and displaced by urban development.

A group of workers are restoring an old building in an abandoned whaling town near Antarctica. Why? That building is where legendary explorer Ernest Shackleton (spoiler!) planned the rescue of his stranded crew, following their harrowing, failed mission to cross Antarctica. Some of the artifacts uncovered will be donated to the South Georgia Museum, which is, predictably, one of the most remote museums in the world.

A pair of flamingos were spotted attacking an inflatable bird floatie on a beach in Aruba. What brand is that floatie? I’m shocked it didn’t pop!

I don’t play many video games, but the reviews of the new Grand Theft Auto VI make me want to splurge on a console, buy an oversized bean bag chair, and laze around in my parents’ basement for a few days. The game is an “astonishing American epic,” the Post writes. The new GTA “will steal your heart,” the Times predicts. Internet providers in New Zealand — which will get access to the game first — are preparing for a surge in internet demand from millions of users. This cultural phenomenon has officially reached Barbenheimer levels.

Executive Briefing

South Korea and China reach FTA breakthrough as Lee and Xi meet in Shenzhen

John Lee

South Korean President Lee Jae Myung and Chinese leader Xi Jinping announced a breakthrough in negotiations to expand bilateral trade in services and strengthen investment protections in Shenzhen on Wednesday. The two countries declared the substantial conclusion of talks that began eight years and eight months ago, opening the way for greater access to China’s services market. Technical drafting, legal review and formal signing remain outstanding before the agreement can take effect.

The proposed agreement covers entertainment, tourism, legal services, retail, construction and finance. It would prohibit certain requirements for foreign investors to transfer technology, extend protections to specified activities before investments are established and restrict governments from reversing some future market-opening measures. Bilateral services trade totaled $38.8 billion in 2024, compared with $272.9 billion in merchandise trade, according to South Korea’s trade ministry.

19 charts that explain the state of AI

The AI boom is getting a little crazy.

Kai Williams

Nov 18

Preview

READ IN APP

Anthropic is scheduled to go public on Thursday in a transaction that will value the AI giant at more than a trillion dollars. OpenAI is expected to follow suit in the new year. Some people question whether these two companies could possibly be worth so much, but they just had nine of the greatest months of revenue growth in business history.

It won’t be all smooth scaling, however. Earlier this month, Democrats won both houses of Congress in an election where many candidates ran in opposition to data centers. When the new Democratic majorities take power in January, they are expected to put AI regulation near the top of their agenda.

AI is already having a big impact in disciplines like math, physics, and cybersecurity. Many people expect the same forces to reshape other disciplines in the coming months — and this might mean job losses across the economy.

To understand the size of these impacts, it’s helpful to get quantitative. So in this article I’ll present 19 charts that demonstrate the large and growing impact AI is having on the United States and the world.

1. Investment spending keeps rising

When I wrote our chart article this time last year, I focused on answering the question “is there an AI bubble?” In the fall of 2025 a lot of people thought AI investment spending had become unsustainable.

Since then, the scale of AI investment has only grown. In the third quarter of 2026, Meta, Amazon, Oracle, Google, and Microsoft had $230 billion in capital expenditures. That’s 118% more than they spent in the third quarter of 2025, and almost as much as these companies spent over all of 2024.

Spending will probably continue to grow. In 2027, analysts expect these companies to have well north of $1 trillion on capital expenditures. Yet as we’ll see in later charts, the case for a bubble seems weaker now than it did a year ago — largely because AI revenue growth has more than kept pace with the growth in investment spending.

2. The AI boom is much bigger than the broadband boom

In last year’s article, I noted that those same five tech giants invested 1.28% of United States GDP in the second quarter of last year. That already made it one of the largest investment booms in American history. Since then, the situation has gotten even more extreme. Full-year 2025 investment spending grew to 1.33% of GDP. And over the first nine months of 2026, capital expenditures from the same five companies were 2.3% of GDP.

There is no 20th Century precedent for this level of infrastructure investment in the United States. It’s much bigger than the Manhattan project, the Apollo Project, or the broadband boom that peaked in 2000. Arguably the only time that the US economy has been so concentrated in one type of investment is during the railroad boom after the Civil War.

There is one caveat to this graph: not all of the tech company capex is being spent in the US. But a large majority of it is. According to estimates by the think tank Epoch AI, the share of global AI compute that’s in the US is more than 70% — and it’s growing. Moreover, many other companies besides these five are making AI-related investments in the US. So however you measure it, the US is experiencing a nearly unprecedented investment boom.

3. (Some) hyperscalers suddenly need outside capital

This time last year, a key not-a-bubble argument was that the biggest tech companies had profits large enough to pay for AI investments. So there was no need for them to raise outside capital. That’s no longer true.

Amazon, Google, Meta, and Oracle now all have capital expenditures that exceed cash flow from operations. For Google, this is the first time this has ever happened in the 22 years it has been a public company.

Even Microsoft, which still spends less in capex than it earns from operations, is feeling the financial strain. In late October, it offered buyouts to 60,000 employees — or over a quarter of the workforce. Some speculated that the software giant needed to free up capital to buy more chips.

The other companies have turned to issuing debt and selling equity. Over the course of 2026, AI companies including Google, Meta, and Oracle have sold or priced more than $300 billion in equity, according to The Information.

4. Startup funding is mostly going to AI

It isn’t just tech companies that are investing heavily in AI: venture capitalists are too. The figures above track the total deal value invested into startups headquartered in the United States. In real terms, the number has grown dramatically for AI startups while stagnating for other startups.

The spike in 2026 is due partly to a small number of huge AI-related fundraising rounds. Anthropic and OpenAI raised $95 billion and $122 billion respectively through the first three quarters of this year. But there are also many smaller companies that have raised money — many have weaker paths to profitability than the large AI companies.

Investor appetite for AI companies may be weakening, however. OpenAI’s most recent fundraising round raised only $11 billion, less than the $30 billion the company was hoping for.

The focus on AI has also led to complaints that it is increasingly difficult for companies not focused on AI to raise money.

5. AI revenues are growing

With all this investment, will AI pay off? One indication is that revenues have risen steadily across the entire ecosystem, to an annualized run rate of $345 billion in October 2026, according to Exponential View. This is a 4.2-fold increase year over year.

One of the biggest winners has been Anthropic, which reached an annualized run rate of $81 billion in October 2026, according to the Wall Street Journal, up from just $9 billion at the beginning of the year. That growth seems to have slowed somewhat — the company’s quarter three growth was much slower than in quarter two — but that may be because some customers switched from Anthropic to OpenAI.

If revenue continues to grow at the current pace — or even a little slower — the massive investments we saw in earlier charts are likely to pay off handsomely. Exponential View argued that Anthropic’s revenue only needs to grow about 2% per month through 2030 to cover its costs. Anthropic has dramatically exceeded that pace for several years in a row.

6. Fewer companies are onboarding to AI …

It’s not guaranteed that revenue will continue to grow at such a fast clip. By some metrics, AI adoption seems to be slowing.

The company Ramp, which processes payments, has published the percentage of a sample of 85,000 customers that pay for various AI services — including ones from OpenAI and Anthropic. OpenAI was long the leader in adoption, but Anthropic caught up in the first half of 2026 as Claude Code exploded in popularity. Today, 45% of Ramp’s sample pay for Anthropic services.

Since July, though, Anthropic’s percentage has barely grown, mirroring OpenAI’s plateau since mid-2025.

7. … but they’re spending more

But this doesn’t necessarily mean that the companies’ revenue has stopped growing — even from Ramp’s customers. In its IPO filing, Anthropic notes that in aggregate, customers who spent money with Anthropic in the third quarter of 2025 spent about 10 times as much in the third quarter of 2026. The number of customers who spent at least $100,000 in the preceding twelve months increased eight-fold from the end of 2025 to September 30, 2026.

That was driven by rapid adoption of Claude Code between mid-2025 and mid-2026. To continue that pace of growth, Anthropic may need to release several more Claude-Code-sized innovations in the coming months.

8. ChatGPT has more than a billion users — but most don’t pay

Consumer usage of chatbots continues to grow. In September, OpenAI announced that more than 1.2 billion people use ChatGPT weekly — up about 50% from this time last year. For comparison, Google Gemini and Meta AI each have about one billion users. Anthropic’s Claude is likely much less, though we don’t have exact figures.

Individual chatbot users use comparatively few tokens compared to agents. On July 31, OpenAI announced that Codex accounted for 63.3% of all tokens used by enterprise users — despite only 17.3% of enterprise users using Codex. (For individual users, Codex accounted for 16.5% of tokens despite only being 0.7% of users.)

And ChatGPT supports a large free tier. Around 100 million users pay for a subscription: about 8.5% of all users. So the company has been investigating advertising: it announced in late August that it had reached $1 billion in annual recurring revenue in ad sales.

9. The chips at the center of the AI buildout

The largest cost for the AI buildout is chips. Basically all of the AI chips that tech companies buy for US use have to be imported first. The most advanced chips are mainly assembled by TSMC in Taiwan.

The chart above is based on trade data from the Census Bureau. This data doesn’t have a specific category corresponding to Nvidia GPUs (or Google’s TPUs), but the red line corresponds to large computers (“automatic data processing machines” minus laptops), a category that includes most GPU and TPU imports. This has spiked to over $500 billion in annualized spending recently — up from $200 billion a year ago. Similarly, imports of computer parts and accessories (HS 8473.30), such as hard drives or power supply units, have more than doubled in the past year.

AT THE SCENE

near Kupyansk, Ukraine

Inside the old gas pipeline turned battlefield

The BBC is the first international broadcaster to enter the pipeline where the subterranean battle is taking place.

There's a new front in the war in Ukraine, and it is underground. For the past seven months Ukrainian forces have been living and fighting Russian troops in an old Soviet gas pipeline in the Kharkiv region.

Jonathan Beale, defence correspondent

With a diameter of just over a metre there's enough room only to crawl. Going underground is now the "only option", says Zanuda, who has helped plan Ukraine's tunnel operation and calls it a new world of fighting. But, he acknowledges, it is hard. "On the surface you always have some room to manoeuvre, but here you can only engage the enemy head-on."

Arriving at the tunnel entrance, the first thing to hit you is the lingering smell of gas and fetid air. Both sides use openings in the pipeline to get to the surface, where most of the fighting takes place.The Russians were the first to exploit the pipe to infiltrate the nearby city of Kupyansk in September 2025. But Ukrainian forces have slowly turned the tables.

What US-backed mineral highway could mean for DR Congo

https://click.email.bbc.com/?qs=ABl7ImQiOjUwNjQsInQiOjYzODcsInMiOjZ9AAYAAAAAB2hyJKN4fvPKeTNtrxfVv1RtQm13exMmVqA5kOGyIJ2qX2E6QBBKLx-oEPlJ6HuCbcyvaHTRLujdvUdlsQwbtzO_-uV7gLNg5LL5a-znwQ The Lobito Corridor links DR Congo's mineral-rich south to Angola's Atlantic coast through the Benguela Railway and the Port of Lobito. Credit: AFP via Getty Images

Global demand for copper and cobalt - essential ingredients in electrical components - is soaring as we transition to cleaner energy. Currently China dominates the world's critical minerals processing capacity, but the US wants to change this. The Lobito Corridor is an American-backed effort to secure access to Africa's critical minerals - transporting them by railway from DR Congo to Angola's Atlantic coast. The battle for control of mineral resources has fuelled decades of conflict in DR Congo - could it now help deliver peace and prosperity?

Taiwan Salon S5E7. Secret Sauce Is The Community: Yun Hai on Telling Taiwan’s Story Through Food, ft. Lisa Cheng Smith and Lillian Lin

By supplying authentic ingredients and telling nuanced stories, Yun Hai encourages people to explore Taiwanese culture, history, and language.

NOVEMBER 2026 I TAIWAN SALON SEASON 5, EPISODE 7

Secret Sauce Is The Community:

Yun Hai on Telling Taiwan’s Story Through Food,

ft. Lisa Cheng Smith and Lillian Lin

“From the very beginning, the project [Yun Hai] is like cultural activism that tells Taiwan’s stories; and hopefully changes the landscape of Taiwan’s standing in the US and the world.”

In the seventh episode of Taiwan Salon Season 5, former GTI Communications Associate Yuchen Lee interviewed Lisa Cheng Smith and Lillian Lin, the CEO and the COO of Yun Hai (雲海)—a Brooklyn-based food business that offers premium Taiwanese ingredients across the United States. Together, they discussed how Yun Hai endeavors to promote the visibility of Taiwanese culture through digital media engagement and community-building.

Lisa and Lillian explained that they position Yun Hai at the top of the “marketing funnel” for Taiwan. By supplying authentic ingredients and telling nuanced stories, Yun Hai encourages people to explore Taiwanese culture, history, and language.
